analysis.one_liner: Blocks EPA from restricting carbon pollution from power plants and factories for two years.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have suspended EPA limits on carbon dioxide and methane from power plants and factories for two years, died in committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2009-2010, the EPA was moving to regulate carbon dioxide and methane under the Clean Air Act, starting with cars and then extending to large stationary sources like power plants, refineries, and factories. This bill would have barred the EPA for two years from taking any Clean Air Act action on those gases for stationary sources — no permits, no performance standards — and would declare that nothing the EPA did in the meantime could make carbon dioxide or methane a regulated pollutant for those sources. Vehicle emission standards were carved out, and reporting and state-requested technical help were allowed. The bill never left the House Energy and Commerce Committee and became moot when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of coal-fired power plants, other large industrial emitters, and coal-producing regions, who would have gotten at least two more years without federal carbon limits, permit requirements, or new performance standards for their facilities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal utilities and large industrial emitters

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the EPA, for two years after enactment, from taking any Clean Air Act action on stationary source permitting or new-source performance standards with respect to carbon dioxide or methane [S2][S3].
It exempts the pending vehicle emission standards from the prohibition, so the EPA's car rules could proceed while power plants and factories got the delay [S2][S3].

It adds a legal backstop: no EPA action during the period could be considered to make carbon dioxide or methane a regulated pollutant for any source other than vehicles, which would have made the delay harder to undo in court [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people living near and downwind of coal plants and large factories, who would wait at least two more years for federal limits on the carbon pollution those facilities emit, and anyone affected by the added emissions during the delay.

drawbacks.text: The delay would have postponed federal limits on carbon dioxide and methane from power plants and other large stationary sources, which are among the biggest emitters of those gases, for two full years [S2][S3].

The bill would not merely pause EPA action; the 'treatment' section would declare that no interim EPA action makes carbon dioxide or methane a regulated pollutant for stationary sources, creating legal cover against regulation that goes beyond a simple time-out [S3].

A fair-minded supporter would argue the pause was meant to give Congress time to write its own climate policy instead of leaving it to EPA rules made case by case through permitting — but that Congressional process had not produced a law, so the practical effect was two more years without either Congressional or EPA limits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered industry a two-year reprieve from carbon rules in exchange for a Congressional process that had no guarantee of producing replacement legislation. The cost fell on the public: two more years of unrestricted carbon emissions from the largest stationary sources, with a legal clause designed to make the pause stick. For the industries it shielded, it was a clear win; for anyone exposed to those emissions, it was a pure loss with no offsetting benefit in the bill itself.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Representative Nick Rahall of West Virginia introduced the bill on March 4, 2010, joined by Representatives Alan Mollohan and Rick Boucher, both also from coal-state districts [S3][S5].
Sixteen members cosponsored the bill — fourteen Democrats and two Republicans [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day it was introduced [S5].
The action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action ever followed the referral [S5].
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and all bills not passed by then expire [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The EPA's authority over carbon dioxide and methane from stationary sources remained intact, and the power plants, refineries, and other large emitters that the bill was written to shield did not get their two-year reprieve. Coal-producing members of Congress did not get the delay their regions' utilities wanted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: EPA carbon rules survived; coal utilities got nothing

for.name: Nick Rahall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to suspend EPA carbon regulation of stationary sources for two years.

for.name: 16 cosponsors
for.role: 14 of 253 House Democrats and 2 of 178 House Republicans

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Henry Waxman (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or reported the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was not organized by party: the sponsor and fourteen of the sixteen cosponsors were Democrats, many from coal-producing districts, while only two Republicans cosponsored [S4].

industries.industry: Coal-fired power plants and other large stationary emitters
industries.note: The bill would have given these facilities a two-year exemption from any new Clean Air Act permitting or performance standards for carbon dioxide and methane, and a legal clause blocking interim EPA action from counting as regulation. The public's cost is two more years of unrestricted emissions from some of the country's largest sources.

Slower cleanup limits on coal-burning utilities means continued demand for coal. The bill's sponsor and cosponsors were concentrated in coal-producing states, and the delay would have protected the fuel those utilities burn.
Refineries and industrial facilities facing permitting requirements for greenhouse gases would have been covered by the same two-year suspension of stationary source rules.
